import numpy as np

class TeachingScene(Scene):
    def setup_layout(self, title_text, lecture_lines):
        # BASE
        self.camera.background_color = "#000000"
        self.title = Text(title_text, font_size=28, color=WHITE).to_edge(UP)
        self.add(self.title)

        # Left-side lecture content (bullets with "-")
        lecture_texts = [Text(line, font_size=22, color=WHITE) for line in lecture_lines]
        self.lecture = VGroup(*lecture_texts).arrange(DOWN, aligned_edge=LEFT).scale(0.8)
        self.lecture.to_edge(LEFT, buff=0.2)
        self.add(self.lecture)

        # Define fine-grained animation grid (4x4 grid on right side)
        self.grid = {}
        rows = ["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F"]  # Top to bottom
        cols = ["1", "2", "3", "4", "5", "6"]  # Left to right

        for i, row in enumerate(rows):
            for j, col in enumerate(cols):
                x = 0.5 + j * 1
                y = 2.2 - i * 1
                self.grid[f"{row}{col}"] = np.array([x, y, 0])

    def place_at_grid(self, mobject, grid_pos, scale_factor=1.0):
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(self.grid[grid_pos])
        return mobject

    def place_in_area(self, mobject, top_left, bottom_right, scale_factor=1.0):
        tl_pos = self.grid[top_left]
        br_pos = self.grid[bottom_right]
        
        # Calculate center of the area
        center_x = (tl_pos[0] + br_pos[0]) / 2
        center_y = (tl_pos[1] + br_pos[1]) / 2
        center = np.array([center_x, center_y, 0])
        
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(center)
        return mobject

        # Data from shared state
        title = "The Core: Bayes' Theorem Formula"
        lecture_lines = [
            "Bayes' Theorem lets us reverse conditional probabilities.",
            "Start with your prior belief in the hypothesis.",
            "Multiply by the likelihood of seeing this evidence.",
            "Divide by the total probability of that evidence.",
            "Now you have the updated posterior probability."
        ]
        self.setup_layout(title, lecture_lines)
        
        # Colors defined in requirements
        PRIOR_COLOR = "#FFFF00"
        LIKELIHOOD_COLOR = "#00FF00"
        EVIDENCE_COLOR = "#00FFFF"
        POSTERIOR_COLOR = "#FF00FF"
        HIGHLIGHT_COLOR = WHITE
        DIM_COLOR = GRAY

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        # Bayes' Theorem lets us reverse conditional probabilities.
        # Write the full Bayes formula P(A|B) = P(B|A)P(A)/P(B).
        
        # Formula parts: 0:P(A|B), 1:=, 2:{, 3:P(B|A), 4:P(A), 5:\over, 6:P(B), 7:}
        formula = MathTex(
            "P(A|B)", "=", "{", "P(B|A)", "P(A)", "\\over", "P(B)", "}"
        )
        
        # Place formula in the center of visual area (spanning B2 to D6 per Issue 41)
        self.place_in_area(formula, "B2", "D6", scale_factor=1.1)
        
        self.play(self.lecture[0].animate.set_color(HIGHLIGHT_COLOR))
        self.play(Write(formula))
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        # Start with your prior belief in the hypothesis.
        # Highlight P(A) in #FFFF00 and label it 'Prior'.

        self.place_at_grid(prior_label, "A5", scale_factor=0.8)

            self.lecture[0].animate.set_color(DIM_COLOR),
            self.lecture[1].animate.set_color(PRIOR_COLOR)

            self.lecture[1].animate.set_color(DIM_COLOR),
            self.lecture[2].animate.set_color(LIKELIHOOD_COLOR)

outline.topic: Bayes' Theorem and the Logic of Independence
outline.target_audience: Undergraduate students or advanced high school students with basic probability knowledge.

sections.title: The Hook: The Detective Dog's Dilemma
sections.content: Introduce the concept of 'updating belief' through a story. A detective dog named 'Sherlock Bones' hears a rustle in the bushes. He thinks there's a 10% chance it's a cat. If it were a cat, his ears would twitch with 90% certainty. His ears just twitched. Does this mean it's definitely a cat? This sets the stage for prior vs. posterior probability.
sections.example: Visual: Sherlock Bones with a thought bubble showing a 'Cat' (10%) and 'Wind' (90%). An animation shows his ears twitching as the 'new evidence'.

sections.title: Prerequisite: Conditional Probability & The Shrinking Universe
sections.content: Explain P(A|B) using a Venn Diagram. Emphasize that 'Given B' means our 'Universe' (Sample Space) shrinks from the whole rectangle to just circle B. We are now looking for the area where A and B overlap within that new, smaller circle.
sections.example: Animation: A large square (Total Probability) fades out, leaving only a glowing circle 'B'. A small slice of 'A' inside 'B' is highlighted to represent P(A|B) = P(A ∩ B) / P(B).

sections.title: Independence: The 'No Influence' Zone
sections.content: Define Independence. If A and B are independent, knowing B happened doesn't change the probability of A. Mathematically: P(A|B) = P(A). This means the 'proportion' of A inside B is the same as A's proportion in the whole universe.
sections.example: Visual: Two circles (A and B) that don't overlap in a way that suggests dependency. If we zoom into B, the percentage of A remains exactly the same as it was in the original square.

sections.title: The Core: Bayes' Theorem Formula
sections.content: Derive Bayes' Theorem by combining the conditional probability formulas. Show how P(A|B) allows us to reverse the condition to find P(B|A). Focus on the components: Prior P(A), Likelihood P(B|A), and Evidence P(B).
sections.example: Graphic: A balance scale. On one side is our 'Prior belief' (P(A)). We add 'Evidence' (the Likelihood ratio) to tip the scale toward the 'Posterior' result.

sections.title: Application: The 'Broken Robot' Test
sections.content: Apply the theorem to a classic false-positive scenario. A 'Quality Control Robot' scans chips. 1% of chips are defective (Prior). The robot is 99% accurate but has a 5% false alarm rate. If the robot beeps, what is the actual chance the chip is broken? This highlights how even 'good' evidence can be misleading if the prior is low.
sections.example: Tree Diagram: Start with 1,000 chips. Branch into 10 Defective and 990 Healthy. Show the robot's 'Beep' paths. Most beeps actually come from healthy chips (False Positives), surprising the learner.

sections.title: Independence in Bayes' Context
sections.content: Briefly explain what happens to Bayes' Theorem if events are independent. If A and B are independent, P(A|B) simply equals P(A). The evidence B becomes 'noise' and doesn't update our belief about A at all.
sections.example: Visual: A 'Bayes Machine' where the input 'Evidence B' passes through a filter. If B is independent of A, the output (Posterior) is identical to the input (Prior).

sections.title: Summary & Key Takeaways
sections.content: Summarize: 1. Bayes' Theorem is a way to update beliefs. 2. Independence means evidence is irrelevant. 3. Always consider the Prior (the base rate) before jumping to conclusions.
sections.example: Final Animation: Sherlock Bones successfully identifies the 'Cat' after combining his twitching ears with the base rate of cats in the neighborhood.

lecture_lines: Bayes' Theorem lets us reverse conditional probabilities.
Start with your prior belief in the hypothesis.
